description: Analyzing and mapping abandoned human technology on the Moon and Mars—including legacy landers, rovers, and hardware. We aim to explore their environmental impact, historical significance, and possibilities for future space recycling or preservation. I am leading background research, content documentation, and building our 7-slide presentation deck. All skill levels welcome!
summary: This project, titled ‘Project Nepali Sharps: Architecture of Tomorrow's Past’ presents a sustainable framework for planetary exploration by combining orbital asset recovery, circular hardware reuse, and proactive autonomous rover defense. By leveraging NASA’s LROC, HiRISE, and PDS imaging systems, the initiative first pinpoints legacy machines across lunar and Martian terrains to determine if they can be revived using targeted, replaceable components. When reactivation is not possible, high-value structural elements—such as titanium frames and wheels—are extracted and repurposed for next-generation machines; the lack of atmospheric humidity in space preserves these metal components in prime condition over long periods. To ensure the longevity of future rovers, the system incorporates an aerodynamic, top-mounted carbon-fiber umbrella mechanism powered by embedded Python code, which uses optical cameras and real-time environmental sensors to automatically deploy during Martian dust storms and retract once the weather clears.
details:
1. Orbital Site Mapping
Our project utilizes high-resolution orbital imaging satellites—specifically the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) on the Moon and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's HiRISE system on Mars—to scan legacy landing sites, assess physical hardware degradation, monitor surface dust accumulation, and verify structural integrity prior to surface deployment. By integrating core open datasets and mission archives, our group establishes a robust foundation designed to support sustainable, long-term space exploration. This orbital mapping methodology allows us to precisely locate abandoned space assets, verify surface coordinates, and track ongoing environmental changes from space.
Furthermore, the Planetary Data System (PDS) is leveraged to access vital mission archives, detailed telemetry data, and comprehensive 3D terrain models. This meticulous data integration does more than just honor the rich history of space exploration; it actively constructs a low-cost, highly sustainable framework tailored for future Moon-to-Mars missions. By systematically identifying legacy hardware debris from orbit, we create a scalable blueprint for circular resource management on extraterrestrial bases, bridging the heritage of historical Apollo and Mars rovers with upcoming Artemis missions and crewed planetary exploration.


2. Dust Mitigation and Array Revival
Our project tackles the practical logistics of off-world sustainability through targeted dust mitigation and array revival strategies, turning dormant space assets into active local resources. To address covered and degraded solar panels (such as those on legacy landers like InSight), the framework implements advanced dust-clearing techniques—utilizing electrostatic dust-clearing principles and mechanical sweeping tools—to clear accumulated regolith and dust layers, aiming to restore basic power generation capabilities where feasible.
Complementing dust removal, this phase focuses on maximizing the utility of stationary hardware through autonomous relay conversion and material harvesting. By equipping inactive landers and rovers with low-power radio transceivers, the initiative breathes new life into abandoned units, transforming them into functional surface communication relay stations for future astronauts and rovers. Additionally, we outline a systematic approach for extracting high-value structural components—such as durable titanium chassis frames, copper wiring, and thermal shielding—directly from historical hardware. Harvesting these materials locally supplies essential repair parts and structural elements for surface habitats, drastically reducing payload launch mass and expensive supply chain costs originating from Earth.


3.NASA Science Alignment
Our group establishes the fundamental NASA Science Alignment of the project by mapping out how open government data and mission archives serve as the baseline for our off-world asset framework. We use the lunar reconnaissance orbiter camera (LORC) for high precision lunar surface image and landing site coordinate verification. Also, our project utilizes the mars reconnaissance orbiters HiRISE system for high resolution martian surface imagery and environment dust tracking. Along with these resources, we use the Planetary Data System (PDS) as a reference for accessing mission data, historical records and 3D terrain information.
Our main idea is to connect the achievements of earlier space missions, such as the Apollo moon landings and the first mars rover missions, with the needs of future space exploration.
Our project honors space heritage by establishing a low-cost data backed road map for moon to mars mission. IT proves that legacy hardware can inform modern interplanetary architectures.


4.Project Impact and Future Vision
Our project outlines the project impact and future vision with focus on two core pillars: sustainable base infrastructure and long-term human space flight impact. We use sustainable base infrastructure by transforming hardware debris into usable building materials and functional surface communication relays. Our project reduces payback launch mass and supply chain cost from Earth for future lunar and Martian missions. Our group works on the long-term human space flight impact, which establishes a scalable blueprint for circular resource management on extraterrestrial bases. Also bridges historical Apollo and Mars rover heritage with upcoming Artemis and crewed planetary exploration.
Additionally, our group project highlights the proactive autonomous dust shield and rover defense system, which protects future Martian and lunar missions from surface dust storms. We designed this project with key features, including optional hazard detection via a high-mounted optical camera to continuously monitor atmospheric clarity and surface dust accumulation in real time, and a deployable carbon fiber umbrella shield that automatically deploys a lightweight carbon fiber umbrella structure when an upcoming dust storm is detected.The complete enclosure expands large enough to completely cover and shield the entire rover body from top to bottom, protecting delicate solar panels, joints, and instruments from high-velocity wind-blown regolith. Our project's automated self-protect system integrates sensors embedded directly on the shell to monitor when the storm has passed and atmospheric conditions stabilize, signaling the mechanism to automatically lift, fold, and stow itself, allowing it to resume normal science operations.
Under verified NASA Open Data archives, our group presentation highlights how the proposed off-world recycling and autonomous rover defense strategies are directly built upon NASA open-access planetary databases. Our key datasets cited include the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbit Camera (LROC) archive for lunar surface terrain mapping and coordinate verification, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) data for Martian surface morphology and dust storm monitoring, and the Planetary Data System (PDS) for historical spacecraft telemetry, mission logs, and 3D surface models. By referencing official NASA repositories (NASA.gov, GPL.NASA.gov, and science.nasa.gov), the initiative establishes high technical credibility, Demonstrating that repurposing abandoned landers and rovers is feasible using real-world orbital telemetry.
Under the final mission synthesis, we bring a compelling close by reinforcing the core takeaway: legacy space hardware left on the Moon and Mars remains not space junk but valuable foundational infrastructure for future exploration.Our project reduces launch mass requirements, lower mission logistics costs, and establishes a circular resource model that connects Apollo and Mars rover habitats directly to the upcoming Artemis missions and crewed planetary expansion by reclaiming these assets.



5.Future Machinery To Solve The Initial Problem
Our project details the Automated Umbrella Deployment and migration system, designed to protect critical rover subsystems during extreme Martian dust storms. We have a front-mounted ESP32 CAM continuously scans the horizon for incoming atmospheric hazards and relays visual feeds to a central microcontroller to achieve full autonomy. Upon hazard confirmation, our central brain signals an L298N motor driver to power dual microelectric linear actuators, smoothly deploying a high-strength carbon fiber and titanium umbrella shield over the rover chassis. We have integrated canopy sensors, specifically a Sharp GP2Y14AU0F dust sensor and a VH750 ambient light sensor, continuously monitor atmospheric clarity and solar illumination. Utilizing programmed digital and logic loops, our system automatically retracts the canopy once baseline clear-sky conditions return, ensuring full operational readiness with minimal manual intervention.
Complementing the hardware schematic, our slide emphasizes the core philosophy of preserving history, building the future. Under Closing the Loop, our project highlights how transforming legacy space debris into functional assets creates a sustainable circular economy for off-world exploration. Under Lasting Impact, we stress that reclaiming Lutrax hardware, while deploying proactive defense ensures safe self-sustaining habitats for Artemis and future planetary missions. Our architecture is supported by validated institutional defenses, including NASA.gov, JPL.NASA, and Science.NASA.gov.
